MUQATIL:57:20/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:57:20/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:57:20/r1.claim: The verse teaches detachment from worldly life, whose play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and accumulation include homes and mounts as well as money and children.

MUQATIL:57:20/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:57:20/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:57:20/r2.claim: Worldly life resembles rain-fed pasture that delights unbelievers, then yellows and becomes dead debris; so does the world for one who prefers it.

MUQATIL:57:20/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:57:20/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:57:20/r3.claim: The Hereafter has severe punishment and God's forgiveness and approval for believers; worldly life is only a passing, deceptive enjoyment.

FARRA:v3p135/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p135/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p135/r3.claim: The hereafter offers either severe punishment or God's forgiveness and approval; الواو here can mean the same choice as أو, as in every orphan and widow.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p454/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p454/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p454/r1.claim: Kuffār here means farmers: they cover the seed with earth after sowing.

TUSTARI:57:20/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:57:20/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:57:20/r1.claim: Worldly life is a sleeping soul and the afterlife is an awake soul.

TUSTARI:57:20/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:57:20/r2.speaker: author
TUSTARI:57:20/r2.claim: The path to salvation begins with knowledge, bears fruit in resisting appetite and avoiding prohibitions, then disciplines the soul to fulfill commands in purity; this makes worship easy and leads to the stations of worshippers and their spiritual tasting.

TUSTARI:57:20/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:57:20/r3.speaker: author
TUSTARI:57:20/r3.claim: A story says Abraham, thirsty in a hot desert, asked an Abyssinian herdsman for water; the man struck a rock and water sprang out.

TUSTARI:57:20/r4.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:57:20/r4.speaker: الله
TUSTARI:57:20/r4.claim: God says He would have removed the heavens and earth at the herdsman’s request because the man wanted nothing in either world but God.

TUSTARI:57:20/r5.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:57:20/r5.speaker: عامر بن عبد القيس
TUSTARI:57:20/r5.claim: Amir ibn Abd Qays says he gave up women and collecting water, while accepting sleep and food as unavoidable needs to manage as best he could.

TAB-FULL:v22p416/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p416/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p416/r1.claim: Worldly life is temporary play, amusement, adornment, mutual boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children; like rain-grown greenery it becomes yellow after its fresh green growth.

TAB-FULL:v22p417/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p417/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v22p417/r1.claim: The plant dries and breaks into dry fragments; the afterlife holds severe punishment for disbelievers and forgiveness and favor for believers.

TAB-FULL:v22p417/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p417/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v22p417/r2.claim: Qatāda says people ultimately come to these two outcomes in the afterlife.

TAB-FULL:v22p417/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v22p417/r3.speaker: بعض أهل العربية
TAB-FULL:v22p417/r3.claim: A grammarian says the afterlife is either punishment or Paradise, and the conjunction wāw functions like aw, “or.”

ZAJJAJ:v5p127#2/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p127#2/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p127#2/r1.claim: Yahīj means that the crop begins to dry and turn yellow; ḥuṭāman means shattered, broken, and gone, illustrating worldly life’s passing.

ZAJJAJ:v5p127#2/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p127#2/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p127#2/r2.claim: Riḍwān is also read riḍwān; ʿĀṣim is reported to have transmitted both the ḍamma and kasra forms, meaning forgiveness for God’s friends and punishment for His enemies.

ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r1.claim: The kāf in kamathali is nominative as an adjective; the clause likens worldly life and its ornaments to rain and its growth.

ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r2.claim: Alternatively, the kāf is nominative as a predicate after another predicate: worldly life and its adornment are like rain whose growth amazes people.

ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r3.claim: Al-kuffār can mean cultivators: if even farmers are impressed by the crop, who know it well, its growth is exceptionally beautiful.

ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p127/r4.claim: Alternatively, al-kuffār means those who disbelieve in God; they are more impressed by worldly adornment than believers.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p362/r1.claim: In innamā, mā prevents anna from governing; if treated as relative, al-ḥayāt and al-dunyā would be accusative, with al-dunyā adjectival and laʿib the predicate.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p362/r2.claim: Worldly life is enjoyed like play, then vanishes along with its adornment and people's boasting of wealth and children.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v4p362/r3.claim: He parses the kāf in kamathali as a nominative adjective, or as a second predicate: people's boasting is like rain.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r4.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v4p362/r4.claim: Al-kuffār may mean farmers, whose admiration shows the crop's great beauty.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r5.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v4p362/r5.claim: Alternatively it means disbelievers, for worldly life pleases them because they reject resurrection.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r6.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p362/r6.claim: Yahīj means that growth begins to yellow; ḥuṭām means broken to pieces.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r7.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v4p362/r7.claim: God compares worldly life and its passing to the crop, then contrasts punishment with forgiveness and divine approval in the next life.

NAHHAS:v4p362/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v4p362/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
NAHHAS:v4p362/r8.claim: A place in Paradise the size of a whip is better than the world and all it contains; the Prophet cites this verse.

SULAMI:v2p310#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r1.speaker: ذو النون
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r1.claim: The world is blameworthy, especially for those who seek it, rely on it, boast in it, or urge others toward it; denouncing it can itself become a practiced trade.

SULAMI:v2p310#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r2.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r2.claim: The world is a house of trial, toil, and desire; whoever exhausts his worldly aims is safe from everything.

SULAMI:v2p310#3/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r3.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r3.claim: The world is what passes away, while the afterlife remains and never perishes.

SULAMI:v2p310#3/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r4.speaker: سهل
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r4.claim: The root of worldly life is ignorance; its branches include bodily pleasures and possessions, and its fruits are sins, punishment, hard-heartedness, and love of sin.

SULAMI:v2p310#3/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r5.speaker: عمر المكي
SULAMI:v2p310#3/r5.claim: God describes worldly life through both praise and blame, using invitation, warning, longing, and caution, as in this verse's depiction of play and amusement.

SULAMI:v2p310#4/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r1.claim: Whatever distracts a servant from the afterlife is worldly life; for different people that distraction may be property, trade, status, work, company, or personal desire.

SULAMI:v2p310#4/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r2.speaker: ذو النون
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r2.claim: Seekers should not pursue the world; if they do, they should not love it, since it is only provision for a journey whose resting place is elsewhere.

SULAMI:v2p310#4/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r3.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r3.claim: Worldly governance relies on power and planning, religious governance on obeying commands and prohibitions, and seeking God on disavowing one's own power.

SULAMI:v2p310#4/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r4.speaker: سهل
SULAMI:v2p310#4/r4.claim: The world is a sleeping self, while the afterlife is an awakened self.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r1.speaker: قتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r1.claim: Play and amusement mean eating and drinking.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r2.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r2.claim: They may bear their ordinary meaning; every play is amusement.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r3.claim: Play may be worldly pursuits and amusement what distracts from the Hereafter; alternatively, play is acquisition and amusement is women.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r4.claim: Adornment may be transient decoration or anything done outside obedience.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r5.claim: Boasting may concern physique and strength or lineage, as Arabs competed over ancestry.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r6.claim: Pre-Islamic people competed in wealth and children, while believers compete in faith and obedience.

MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v5p480/r7.claim: The crop yellows, becomes chaff, and disappears after beauty, like the disbeliever's world.

QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r1.claim: Worldly life is transient, distracting, tempting but unsatisfying, and diverted from right guidance; it breeds adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children.

QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r2.claim: In the parable, “disbelievers” means farmers: the crop delights them, then dries and breaks apart.

QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r3.claim: The afterlife brings severe punishment to disbelievers and forgiveness and approval from God to believers.

QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p290/r4.claim: The world is contemptible, its pursuer lower still, and the one who competes for it lower yet; it is carrion, and the miser is its worst inhabitant.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says worldly adornment consists of things people use to beautify themselves that God does not love or approve.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r2.claim: A disbeliever spends life adorning himself for this world rather than working for the afterlife; saying his life is adornment means he spends it on adornment, not that they are identical.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says people boast to relatives and neighbors.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says people amass unlawful wealth to boast and lord their money, servants, and children over God's allies.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r5.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r5.claim: Al-Zajjaj says the simile's كاف can be nominative either as an adjective for play and its following terms or as another predicate.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r6.speaker: عبد الله ومجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r6.claim: Abdullah and Mujahid explain the farmers who admire the plants as cultivators.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r7.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r7.claim: Al-Azhari says Arabs call the farmer a kāfir because he covers the seed he sows with soil; a plant admired by cultivators is at its most attractive.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r8.speaker: الأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300#2/r8.claim: An alternative takes الكفار literally as unbelievers, who are especially impressed by worldly adornment and crops; the source says much of this analysis is Abu Ishaq's.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r1.claim: The author objects to later exegetes who interpret worldly life as its possessions and attractions: دنيا describes the life in this world, not the life itself as a possession.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r2.claim: Human beings have a life in this world and a second life in the afterlife; the condemned description concerns people whose life is not spent in God's obedience.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says whatever is done for other than God is false and delusive.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p300/r4.claim: This life is called play and amusement because it soon passes away and, when detached from obedience, is false and delusive.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r1.claim: The author says the plant is what grows from rain and refers the remaining explanation to 39:21.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r2.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r2.claim: The scholars of meaning say the verse turns people away from worldly work and urges work for the afterlife; this describes disbelievers and warns believers against that kind of life.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r3.claim: The mention of severe punishment in the afterlife clarifies that people whose lives take this form face that punishment.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r4.speaker: مقاتل وابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r4.claim: Muqatil and Ibn Abbas assign punishment to God's enemies and forgiveness and favor to His obedient allies.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r5.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r5.claim: Al-Zajjaj likewise says forgiveness is for God's allies and punishment for His enemies.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r6.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p301/r6.claim: Al-Farra says the afterlife contains either punishment or Paradise.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p302/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p302/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p302/r1.claim: Worldly life is delusive enjoyment for someone who works for it without working for the afterlife; the enjoyment ends and vanishes.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p302/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p302/r2.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v21p302/r2.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says delusive enjoyment is whatever distracts from pursuing the afterlife; what does not distract is provision toward something better.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:57:19-20/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:57:19-20/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:57:19-20/r3.claim: Worldly life is passing play, diversion, adornment, boasting, and competition in wealth and children. Like rain-grown crops that yellow, dry, and crumble, people age, die, and decay; the afterlife holds punishment for disbelievers and forgiveness and approval for God's friends. Here “the disbelievers” means farmers.

JISHUMI:v9p6793/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r1.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r1.claim: Ghayth may mean a cloud or, in Abu Ali's view, rain.

JISHUMI:v9p6793/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r2.claim: The comparison may be to vegetation struck by rain that delights farmers with its beauty, or to disbelievers who attach themselves to worldly display, unlike believers who prefer the afterlife.

JISHUMI:v9p6793/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r3.claim: The plant dries, yellows after being green, then breaks into chaff that displeases the eye after first delighting it.

JISHUMI:v9p6793/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r4.claim: The afterlife brings severe punishment to the persistent and forgiveness and divine pleasure to believers and penitents.

JISHUMI:v9p6793/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v9p6793/r5.claim: Worldly life is deceptive enjoyment because its attractive appearance conceals an opposite inner reality and outcome; the phrase also means people's work in gathering and acquiring it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r1.claim: Worldly life’s play has no lasting result, amusement passes, adornment is appearance, and people boast and compete in wealth and children.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r2.claim: The life is like rain whose growth impresses farmers, then dries, yellows, and breaks apart.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r3.speaker: مقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r3.claim: The severe punishment is for God’s enemies; forgiveness and approval are for His allies and obedient people.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#2/r4.claim: The transient harvest shows worldly life is deceptive enjoyment.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#3/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#3/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p39#3/r1.claim: Worldly life is delusive enjoyment for one occupied in it while seeking the Hereafter; used as a means, it carries one toward what is better.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r1.claim: The verse warns about worldly life; annamā fills the two slots expected after knowledge even though it prevents the verb from governing, and the following clause retains its sentence form.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r2.claim: Worldly life here means its characteristic activities and thoughts, excluding obedience and necessities that sustain worship; the pursuits of kings after poverty show how these concerns amount to play.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r3.claim: Adornment is an external embellishment, mutual boasting concerns lineage and wealth, and multiplication is desire for worldly abundance that grants status by pre-Islamic standards.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r4.claim: The rain parable traces a person from growth, strength, wealth, children, and admiration into aging, weakness, illness, loss, death, and disappearance, like lush growth that dries and breaks apart.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r5.speaker: بعض أهل التأويل
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p266#2/r5.claim: Some take kuffār here as disbelievers, who are especially enamored of worldly beauty; others take it as farmers who cover seed in the earth and can judge good growth.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r1.claim: Hāja means the crop dried and turned yellow; ḥuṭām is an intensive form meaning crushed or broken apart.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r2.claim: The verse mentions punishment before forgiveness and approval to put warning first, since people should first become safe from fear before extending hope.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r3.speaker: عاصم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r3.claim: A report from ʿĀṣim gives ḍamma to the rāʾ in riḍwān.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r4.speaker: عكرمة وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p267/r4.claim: Matāʿ al-ghurūr means enjoyment that seems great only to the deceived; ʿIkrima and others identify it with fragile glass vessels, like worldly life.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:57:19-20/r10.claim: People boast of worldly things to their peers and neighbors.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:57:19-20/r11.claim: People exhaust their lives collecting wealth, children, and servants for rivalry and to lord those advantages over God's friends.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r12.speaker: الزجاج
TABRISI:57:19-20/r12.claim: ‘Farmers’ is a possible sense of kāfir here, since they cultivate and cover seed; alternatively the word means unbelievers, who delight more in worldly life.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r13.speaker: مقاتل
TABRISI:57:19-20/r13.claim: The severe punishment in the hereafter is for God's enemies, while forgiveness and approval are for His friends and obedient people.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r14.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TABRISI:57:19-20/r14.claim: Worldly life is deceptive provision for whoever neglects the afterlife; for one who seeks it, worldly life is a provision carrying him to something better.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r15.speaker: author
TABRISI:57:19-20/r15.claim: Another explanation makes worldly activity itself deceptive provision, ephemeral like the stages of plant growth in the parable.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:57:19-20/r6.claim: Worldly life is like play and amusement because it quickly vanishes without permanence.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r7.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:57:19-20/r7.claim: Every form of play is amusement.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:57:19-20/r8.claim: Alternatively, play is what people desire in worldly life and amusement is what distracts them from the afterlife.

TABRISI:57:19-20/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:57:19-20/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:57:19-20/r9.claim: Adornment is what people decorate themselves with, or the world's appearance that delights its people before disappearing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r1.claim: Worldly life is a deception that soon passes away.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r2.speaker: بعض المفسرين
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r2.claim: Some interpreters take the description specifically as the unbeliever's life, spent in play, adornment, rivalry, and accumulation while neglecting the afterlife.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r3.claim: The rain parable depicts crops that first delight the farmers, then dry, yellow, and break into fragments.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r4.claim: Kuffār here means farmers: the sower covers the seed with earth, and the crop grows from the rain.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r5.claim: The worldly-life parable was already explained in the parable of worldly life in Yūnus and al-Kahf.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p171#2/r6.claim: The afterlife holds severe punishment for God's enemies and forgiveness and approval for His allies and obedient servants.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r1.claim: Boasting is over perishable attributes such as lineage, strength, power, and armies, all of which pass away.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains accumulation of wealth and children as gathering wealth in God's displeasure, boasting against His allies, and spending it in what displeases Him.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r3.claim: Because worldly life consists of these fleeting conditions, one should turn from it toward what builds the afterlife.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r4.claim: Ghayth means rain; the comparison may grammatically modify the list of worldly pursuits or serve as a second predicate, as al-Zajjāj says.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r5.claim: Ibn Masʿūd takes the 'disbelievers' delighted by the plants to mean farmers; al-Azharī explains that Arabs call a farmer a kāfir because he covers seed with soil.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r6.claim: An alternative takes the word as unbelievers, who are more captivated by worldly adornment and crops because they see no happiness beyond this life.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r7.claim: The afterlife offers lasting punishment to those absorbed in worldly life, or forgiveness and God's pleasure to His obedient allies, the highest degrees of reward.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r8.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
RAZI-FULL:v29p203#2/r8.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says worldly life is delusive when it distracts from the afterlife, but an excellent means when it leads one to seek God's pleasure and the afterlife.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r1.claim: The verse's main purpose is to belittle worldly life and exalt the afterlife: worldly play, diversion, adornment, boasting, and accumulation are fleeting, while the afterlife brings lasting punishment or God's favor.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r2.claim: Worldly life itself is wise, purposeful, and a primary blessing, as shown by God's creation of a vicegerent, creation of life and death, rejection of purposelessness, and naming life first among blessings; blame falls on using it for Satan and whim instead of obedience.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r3.claim: Life is called play because children labor at it only for their effort to end without benefit; it is called diversion because youthful pleasures leave regret, lost time and wealth, and intensified longing.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r4.claim: Adornment is likened to women's pursuit of beautifying what is ugly and repairing a building already headed for ruin; an incidental improvement cannot overcome the world's inherent transience.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the unbeliever spends life seeking worldly adornment and does no work for the afterlife; the cited verse describes life as heedlessness.

RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r6.speaker: الشاعر
RAZI-FULL:v29p203/r6.claim: The poem sums up worldly life as heedlessness and neglect.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r1.claim: Believers also have branches of worldly desire, but these become fewer and subtler when they remember the hereafter.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r2.claim: Grammatically, the kāf of the parable is nominative as an adjective.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r3.claim: The crop dries after greening, turns yellow, and becomes broken chaff, just as the disbeliever's worldly life ends.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r4.claim: The severe punishment in the hereafter is for disbelievers; it is good to pause there and begin the forgiveness clause as applying to believers.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r5.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r5.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads the clauses as alternatives—either punishment or forgiveness—so one should not pause after “severe.”

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r6.claim: The closing statement confirms that worldly life deceives disbelievers, while for a believer it is provision and a passage to Paradise.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21#2/r7.claim: Another reading takes worldly-life work as deceptive provision, urging people away from worldly labor and toward the hereafter.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r1.claim: The connection is that fear of death may keep people from striving; since worldly life ends, they should not neglect God's command to preserve what will not last.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r10.speaker: بعض المتأخرين
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r10.claim: A later scholar maps play to children, amusement to young men, adornment to women, boasting to peers, and accumulation to prosperous landowners.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r11.speaker: علي
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r11.claim: ʿAlī tells ʿAmmār worldly enjoyments are six: food, drink, clothing, scent, transport, and sex, each containing some low or dangerous feature; the point is the world's frailty.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r12.claim: Worldly life resembles vegetation grown by rain: it delights onlookers while green, then quickly turns to chaff and disappears.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r13.claim: Al-kuffār in the parable means farmers, because they cover the seed; their admiration for flourishing crops represents the highest worldly beauty.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r14.claim: Another good interpretation takes al-kuffār as unbelievers, who are more captivated by worldly adornment than believers; worldly glorification originates and appears among them.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r2.claim: The particle mā may be extra: worldly life is empty play and amusement that ends.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r3.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r3.claim: Qatāda glosses play and amusement as eating and drinking.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r4.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r4.claim: Mujāhid says play in ordinary usage is amusement.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r5.claim: Other glosses make play attachment to the world and amusement whatever distracts from the hereafter; another pairs play with acquisition and amusement with women.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r6.claim: Adornment is what people decorate themselves with; disbelievers beautify worldly life without working for the afterlife, as do people adorning themselves outside God's obedience.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r7.claim: Boasting may concern worldly possessions, physical form and strength, or ancestry, as in Arab boasting about forefathers.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r8.claim: The Prophet says God revealed that people should be humble, neither oppressing nor boasting over one another; he also called genealogical boasting one of four surviving traits of ignorance.

QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:57:20-21/r9.claim: Pre-Islamic people competed in property and children, whereas believers compete in faith and obedience.

BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r1.claim: Worldly play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and accumulation are trivial if they do not serve the afterlife: futile labor, distraction, fine clothing and homes, lineage, numbers, and goods.

BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r2.claim: The rain-grown plant’s rise, yellowing, and collapse depicts worldly life’s rapid passing and scant benefit; الكفار may mean farmers or unbelievers, who admire appearances because believers infer the Creator while unbelievers remain with sensation.

BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r3.claim: The afterlife holds severe punishment, forgiveness, and divine approval; forgiveness and approval belong to those who turn toward it rather than seek only worldly life.

BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:57:20/r4.claim: Worldly life is only deceptive enjoyment for someone who pursues it without seeking the afterlife.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r1.claim: The stages of worldly life resemble children's play, young men's amusement, women's adornment, elders' boasting, and farmers' rivalry in wealth and children.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r2.claim: Rain-grown plants flourish, then wither and become debris; the world's brief beauty and little lasting benefit are like such vegetation.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r3.claim: The “disbelievers” delighted by the plants may be literal deniers of God's favor or, by another reading, farmers.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p218#4/r4.claim: The plants' ruin is a punishment for ingratitude, as happened to the garden owners and the owner of the two gardens.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r1.claim: The afterlife holds severe punishment for unbelievers and forgiveness and approval from God for believers; these are grave realities unlike worldly amusements.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r2.claim: The comparative kāf phrase is a predicate: worldly life is like rain-grown vegetation; it is deceptive when relied upon.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r3.speaker: ذو النون
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r3.claim: Dhū al-Nūn advises seekers not to seek or love the world: provisions come from it, but the place of rest is elsewhere.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p219/r4.claim: Since this life is small and the next great, people should hasten toward forgiveness from punishment and entrance into Paradise.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r10.claim: The transient world is contrasted with the enduring hereafter, where severe punishment stands alongside God’s forgiveness and good pleasure.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r4.claim: The verse describes the dominant worldly life as transient pursuits with little lasting benefit; obedience and necessities that sustain life are excluded.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r5.claim: Play and amusement resemble the lives of the wealthy; adornment improves what is external, while mutual boasting and rivalry in wealth and children are trivial beside the real, immense matters of the afterlife.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r6.claim: Most read tafākhur with nunation and naṣb on baynakum; al-Sulamī reads it in an iḍāfa construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī compares the world’s quick passing and little benefit to rain-fed growth that flourishes, then yellows and crumbles as punishment for ingratitude, like the garden stories.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r8.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya likens a person’s rise through strength, wealth, children, and status followed by aging, illness, loss, and death to lush growth that dries, breaks, and scatters.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p109/r9.claim: Al-kuffār may be farmers who cover seed, singled out as experts in crops, or unbelievers who admire worldly beauty most; ḥuṭām is an intensive form, and one reading has muṣfāran.

SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r1.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r1.claim: The common form تفاخر is indefinite and either described by the following adverbial phrase or governs it; al-Sulami annexes it to بينكم.

SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r2.claim: كمثل غيث may be circumstantial from لعب treated as an adjective, predicate of an omitted topic, or predicate after خبر; Ibn Atiyya's adjectival parse is unclear, and Makkī's restriction to تفاخر is questionable.

SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r3.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r3.claim: A reading مصفارا derives from اصفار and is more emphatic than مصفر.

SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:57:20/r4.claim: وفي الآخرة is a fronted predicate; severe punishment is paired with two goods, forgiveness and approval, like the proverb of one hardship and two eases.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r1.claim: Worldly life is a brief, deceptive provision for one who relies on it and imagines there is no other abode or resurrection; compared with the Hereafter it is insignificant.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r2.claim: A report says a whip’s-width place in Paradise is better than the world and all it contains; Ibn Kathir notes that the report is authentic without the added wording quoted here.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r3.speaker: عبد الله
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24#2/r3.claim: The Prophet said Paradise is nearer to each person than a sandal strap, and so is the Fire; al-Bukhari alone gives this route.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r1.claim: For worldly people, worldly life amounts to play, distraction, adornment, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children, as another verse describes desire for worldly goods.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r2.claim: The transient life is compared to rain that comes after people have despaired of it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r3.claim: The crop delights its cultivators, just as worldly life delights disbelievers, who are especially attached to it; the green crop yellows and breaks into dry fragments.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r4.claim: The crop’s decline illustrates both worldly life and human aging, from fresh youth through weakening maturity to frail old age.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p24/r5.claim: The Hereafter brings either severe punishment or forgiveness and God’s good pleasure; the present life is only a deceptive enjoyment.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r2.claim: Worldly life is play, distraction, adornment, rivalry, and accumulation of wealth and children, all of which vanish.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r3.claim: Play is fruitless activity, while amusement delights and occupies people until it passes away.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r4.claim: Adornment pleases the eye and soul; rivalry breeds arrogance, envy, and enmity, and accumulation supplies the grounds for pride.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r5.claim: Human life rises from childhood to strength, wealth, family, and social pleasure, then declines into aging, illness, loss, and death.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r6.claim: At death a person is soon forgotten, while others inherit and enjoy the wealth and adornments he prized.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p451/r7.claim: The world is contemptible, its pursuer more contemptible, and those competing over it are like seekers after carrion.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r1.speaker: القشيري
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r1.claim: Al-Qushayrī defines blameworthy worldly life as anything that distracts a servant from the hereafter.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r2.claim: The rain parable likens worldly attractions to a crop that amazes farmers, called kāfirūn because they cover seed and resemble those who conceal faith.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r3.claim: A believer may admire the crop but recalls God’s power and the afterlife, so admiration leads to gratitude and obedience.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r4.claim: The crop soon dries, yellows, and crumbles, illustrating how worldly life loses its appearance and substance.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r5.claim: The afterlife brings severe punishment to those who take worldly goods wrongly and turn away from remembrance, since worldly delusion causes their punishment.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r6.claim: Forgiveness is for believers who remember God and repent; divine approval is for the highest rank, those who spend their effort in gratitude.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r7.claim: Worldly activity used for faith, obedience, and reflection becomes provision for lasting joy; neglecting God’s due leaves enduring regret.

BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v7p452/r8.claim: Worldly enjoyment is deceptive because its pleasure is small beside the harm it brings.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r1.claim: ‘Like rain’ can be an accusative circumstantial phrase, an omitted predicate, or a second predicate for worldly life.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r10.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r10.claim: Human boasting over others is blameworthy because it shows ignorance of one’s own reality.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r11.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r11.speaker: بعض الكبار
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r11.claim: The seven desires in 3:14 are reduced to five here, to two in 47:36, and finally to one: desire (hawā).

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r2.claim: Ghayth is needed, beneficial rain in drought, whereas matar is a general term for rain.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r3.speaker: الأزهري
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r3.claim: Arabs call farmers kuffār because they cover seeds with earth; the root also denotes covering and occurs in words for disbeliever, grave, and night.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r4.claim: Here kuffār means disbelievers: believers move from admiring beauty to its Creator, while disbelievers remain absorbed in the beauty itself.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r5.claim: Adornment is sometimes withheld, as at weddings, to protect spiritually vulnerable hearts.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r6.claim: ‘Then it withers’ means the plant dries after freshness from a heavenly or earthly blight; yellowing accompanies drying, and ḥuṭām is broken fragments.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r7.claim: Worldly things that do not lead to lasting victory are illusory, of little benefit, and quickly gone; the plant simile captures that transience.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r8.speaker: علي رضي الله عنه
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r8.claim: People are asleep and awaken when they die; the saying illustrates worldly life’s transience.

BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303#2/r9.claim: Natural attraction makes adornment worldly and blameworthy without making it unlawful; pursuing it at God’s command makes it praiseworthy divine adornment.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303/r1.claim: Worldly pastime absorbs people and distracts them from the afterlife’s important deeds; adornment means beautiful clothes, mounts, and homes.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303/r2.claim: Boasting is competition over ancestry and status, especially possessions and rank, which lie outside a person; multiplication means competing in numbers of wealth and children, especially to outdo God’s friends.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303/r3.claim: Worldly play and joy soon vanish into grief and sorrow; beauty falls away, while boasting and accumulation disappear like sparks of fire.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303/r4.claim: An alternative comparison likens play to children’s play, adornment to women’s adornment, boasting to peers’ rivalry, and accumulation to farmers’ competition.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r5.speaker: علي
BURSEVI:v9p303/r5.claim: Ali told Ammar not to grieve over the world’s six goods: food, drink, clothing, scent, mounts, and sex, each represented by humble or dangerous examples such as honey as a fly’s spit and musk as deer’s blood.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r6.speaker: النبي
BURSEVI:v9p303/r6.claim: The Prophet compared himself and the world to a rider who rests briefly in a tree’s shade on a hot day, then departs and leaves it behind.

BURSEVI:v9p303/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p303/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p303/r7.claim: A Persian couplet says the world offers no hope of lasting loyalty or permanence.

BURSEVI:v9p304/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p304/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p304/r1.claim: Severe punishment awaits those absorbed in worldly life without seeking the hereafter; forgiveness and divine pleasure await those who turn toward it.

BURSEVI:v9p304/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p304/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p304/r2.claim: A Persian couplet calls the worldly seeker deluded, the hereafter-seeker a hireling, and the one detached from both a seeker of light itself.

BURSEVI:v9p304/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p304/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p304/r3.claim: Good intention can turn a permissible act into worship; a report credits someone who dies asleep after intending night prayer with its reward, and says the same of one setting out for jihad or pilgrimage.

BURSEVI:v9p304/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p304/r4.speaker: بعض الكبار
BURSEVI:v9p304/r4.claim: A major Sufi says sound inwardness and intention can bring the good works intended.

BURSEVI:v9p304/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p304/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p304/r5.claim: Cooks and bakers can turn ordinary work into worship by intending to benefit people; earners should use their income to serve people and support obedience to God.

BURSEVI:v9p304/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v9p304/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v9p304/r6.claim: Serving creatures or thanking a benefactor under God’s command does not compromise servitude to God.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r1.claim: Worldly life is play with no fruit beyond toil, distraction from serious concerns, adornment without intrinsic honor, boasting in ancestry, and competing in numbers, wealth, and children.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r10.claim: Yahīj can mean the plant reaches its utmost growth or, alternatively, dries after being green and fresh.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r11.claim: The plant then appears yellow after having looked fresh; one reading is muṣfārran, and the shift from “it yellows” may signal that yellowing is not simultaneous with maturation or is obvious to all.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r12.claim: The noun kāf may be accusative as a circumstantial phrase linked to “play,” or nominative as a second predicate with an omitted “likeness of life.”

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r13.claim: The plant's short cycle compresses the many years of worldly life into less than a year, showing how quickly it disappears.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r14.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r14.claim: After worldly life is disparaged, the afterlife is magnified to encourage lasting bliss and warn against painful punishment; punishment is mentioned first as a consequence of immersion in worldly pursuits.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r15.claim: Pairing forgiveness and favor against one punishment signals mercy's predominance, like the saying that one hardship cannot overcome two eases.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r2.claim: Adornment means fine clothes, handsome mounts, and lofty homes, which give no inherent distinction.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r3.claim: The boasting is over old ancestors, while accumulation concerns numbers and possessions.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r4.speaker: السلمي
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r4.claim: Al-Sulamī reads tafākhur baynikum with genitive construction.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r5.claim: The rain-growth comparison shows how quickly worldly beauty fades; the next part warns of severe punishment or immense forgiveness and favor in the afterlife.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r6.claim: Ibn Masʿūd explains the “kuffār” who admire the crop as farmers, since they cover seeds in the earth.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r7.claim: Alternatively, kuffār means unbelievers, who are more captivated by worldly decoration; a believer transfers wonder from what is seen to its Creator.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r8.speaker: أبو نواس
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r8.claim: Abū Nuwās's narcissus poem pictures silver eyes and gold on emerald stems as witnesses that God has no partner, illustrating how beauty points beyond itself.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p184#2/r9.claim: A disbeliever, by contrast, does not move thought beyond sensory experience and is wholly absorbed in admiration.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r1.claim: Not describing punishment as “from God” while explicitly attaching forgiveness and favor to God further signals mercy's predominance and that good is the primary aim.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r2.claim: Worldly life is delusive enjoyment for someone who rests in it instead of using it as a means to the afterlife.

ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r3.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
ALUSI-FULL:v27p185/r3.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the world is delusive enjoyment if it distracts from the afterlife, but an excellent provision and means when it leads to God's pleasure and the next life.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r1.claim: Worldly life spent without seeking the hereafter is a fleeting life that deceives and exhausts, with no lasting fruit.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r10.claim: The afterlife offers severe punishment for absorption in worldly life, but also divine forgiveness that covers sins and erases hardship.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r11.claim: Divine pleasure is greater than every pleasure: the believer is both accepted by God and content with Him, an enduring perfection of joy.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r12.claim: Forgiveness and divine pleasure are promised to believers who do not make worldly life their goal and instead work for the hereafter.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r13.claim: Mentioning forgiveness and divine pleasure alongside punishment signals that mercy predominates.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r14.claim: Worldly life is a deceptive provision: it seems pleasant but ends in grief, pain, and punishment.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r15.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r15.speaker: Sa‘îd b. Cübeyr
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r15.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explains that worldly provision is deceptive because it distracts people from seeking the hereafter.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r16.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r16.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r16.claim: Worldly goods become excellent provision when used as a means to seek God’s pleasure and the goods of the hereafter.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r17.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r17.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r17.claim: Believers should not be carried away by temporary pleasures; they should work for the hereafter from love of forgiveness and divine pleasure as well as fear of punishment.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r2.claim: Play absorbs effort but ends in nothing whether one wins or loses.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r3.claim: Diversion keeps people from useful work, duty, and livelihood, and merely wastes time.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r4.claim: Adornment is outward display, confers no intrinsic honor, and deceives the heedless through clothes and finery.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r5.claim: Mutual boasting means competing in pride, claiming superiority through external things such as lineage; pride relies on things outside oneself.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r6.claim: People compete to accumulate wealth and children as a source of pride.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r7.claim: Those who live solely for the world make all their efforts serve these distractions and contests.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r8.claim: “Kuffār” can mean unbelievers in its familiar religious sense, but Elmalılı prefers Ibn Masʿūd’s reported sense of farmers, from the root meaning to cover seed with soil; the wording also alludes to unbelievers’ animal life.

ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:57:20-25#2/r9.claim: The crop first delights the farmers, then matures, yellows, and becomes dry chaff, illustrating worldly life’s decline.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r3.claim: After urging charity, the verse counters miserliness driven by preserving wealth for worldly pleasures: worldly life passes away, while life should secure lasting afterlife bliss and protection from punishment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r4.claim: “Know” opens the exhortation in the same way as the earlier command concerning God reviving the earth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r5.claim: An open hamza in annama still conveys restriction; the six descriptions characterize the dominant concerns of most people, not every possible human act.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p400/r6.claim: The generalization leaves out those God preserves, whose lives serve Him through piety, benefit, kindness, support of truth, teaching virtue, and just law.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r1.claim: Adornment is especially common in youth as people respond to aging; women may seek beauty among both women and men, not merely to attract men.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r2.claim: Adornment pervades worldly life, including homes and clothing, and can be physical or moral, the latter resembling the juristic category of embellishing interests.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r3.claim: Pride is self-praising speech; its reciprocal form suits boasting between people, and people boast of truly good qualities or falsely praised customs and deeds.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r4.claim: False boasting can celebrate extravagance in wine, gambling, fornication, murder, or unjust raiding; boasting is most common in mature adulthood and can breed envy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p402/r5.claim: Takathur is an intensive reciprocal form: people compete to possess more of what they value; the usage later broadened to seeking abundance without direct rivalry.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r1.claim: Fi in “in wealth and children” can mean because of them or figuratively treat them as a setting in which people accumulate more.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r2.claim: Human life was designed as a means for souls to rise toward their angelic potential, as in the creation of a vicegerent on earth; people diverted that design from guidance toward eternal life.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r3.claim: The proper outcome is a good life and reward for faithful righteous action, as the author links to the verse promising the best reward.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r4.claim: The simile can be a new sentence with an omitted subject, “it is like rain,” or a circumstantial phrase where kamathal means “like the state of.”

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r5.claim: The composite image compares people’s attractive, varied worldly states and their rapid passing to vegetation that rain makes flourish before it yellows and breaks apart.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p403/r6.claim: Vegetation is the central comparison; rain is included to portray the stages from their beginning and lend the scene beauty, as in Kaʿb b. Zuhayr’s description of water mixed with wine.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r1.claim: Exegetes commonly gloss yahīj as drying, but the author notes they supplied no Arabic poetic evidence; al-Raghib and al-Asas describe yellowing or beginning to dry.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r2.claim: He prefers “thickens and approaches dryness”: the root suggests agitation, and thickening crops rustle as they move, marking the onset of drying; al-Nabigha’s verse illustrates the root’s sense of stirring.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r3.claim: Thumma marks rank in the sequence because yellowing most clearly signals impending disappearance; fa marks the near-immediate yellowing that accompanies drying.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r4.claim: Ḥuṭām means broken fragments; the crop’s stages portray worldly youth, maturity, old age, decline, and eventual extinction.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p405/r5.claim: The composite simile also permits matching individual stages: life’s arrival, full maturity, early decline, and loss of strength and wealth correspond to the crop’s growth, thickening, yellowing, and shattering.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r1.claim: Actions done for God belong to the afterlife in meaning and only appear to fall under this worldly simile; good works and learning do not decay while pursued, and some grow over time.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r2.claim: The contrast with the afterlife warns and encourages; forgiveness and divine approval name spiritual bliss, which entails bodily pleasure suited to embodied human beings.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r3.claim: Divine approval grants the fullest delight, while forgiveness removes what could impede it; bodily pleasures are ultimately perceived by the spirit.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r4.claim: “Worldly life is only deceptive enjoyment” contrasts the two outcomes; the omitted noun is worldly conditions, and the restriction describes the usual experience of those who seek them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p406/r5.claim: Ghūrūr is deception: presenting something harmful, which a sensible person would avoid, as beneficial and desirable; the genitive expresses the eventual consequence of being deceived.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p407/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p407/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v27p407/r1.claim: This conclusion recaps the passage from 57:12 and urges gaining afterlife bliss while warning against worldly adornment; it foregrounds the desired encouragement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p519/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p519/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p519/r8.claim: Although directly addressed to polytheists, the warning teaches Muslims to resist love of wealth when it distracts from good and to fear death arriving during heedlessness.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r4.claim: Religious piety proceeds through fear, hope, or love; the verse about worldly deception and the hereafter’s punishment, forgiveness, and divine approval grounds these motives.

TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:22-34#24/r5.claim: People differ in disposition: most worship from fear of punishment, while others act piously in hope of forgiveness and Paradise.

TABATABAI:57:19-20/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r2.claim: The passage contrasts the best and worst groups while leaving sinful believers between them, arousing both fear and hope so they choose salvation.

TABATABAI:57:19-20/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r3.claim: The five attractions are play, distraction, adornment, boasting in lineage or status, and accumulation of wealth and children; all are transient appearances without real spiritual good.

TABATABAI:57:19-20/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r4.claim: Play is an ordered act toward an imagined goal, amusement distracts from what matters, adornment adds beauty, boasting is pride in lineage or standing, and multiplication concerns wealth and children.

TABATABAI:57:19-20/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r5.speaker: الشيخ البهائي
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r5.claim: Al-Baha'i maps the five attractions onto life's stages: play in childhood, amusement in youth, adornment in adulthood, boasting at middle age, and wealth and children in old age.

TABATABAI:57:19-20/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:19-20/r6.claim: The rain comparison shows worldly adornment that delights people, then withers, yellows, and becomes debris, soon stripped away.

TABATABAI:57:20-21/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r1.claim: Al-ghayth is rain, al-kuffar means cultivators, yahīj describes movement or growth, and al-hutam is brittle, broken dry vegetation.

TABATABAI:57:20-21/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r2.claim: Worldly life resembles rain whose attractive crop grows to its fullest, yellows, then breaks apart and is scattered by winds.

TABATABAI:57:20-21/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r3.claim: Forgiveness precedes divine approval because cleansing the place of sins prepares it to receive approval; calling forgiveness from God hints it is the primary aim, while punishment follows human departure from servitude.

TABATABAI:57:20-21/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r4.claim: Worldly life is a pleasure whose enjoyment deludes the person attached to it; the afterlife contrast warns hearers to choose forgiveness and approval over punishment.

TABATABAI:57:20-21/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:57:20-21/r5.claim: The closing warning awakens people so worldly life, especially its delusive attractions, will not deceive them.

ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n29/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n29/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n29/r1.claim: Razi stresses that worldly life is not intrinsically contemptible: God created it meaningfully, and it is a positive gift and potential source of blessings.

ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n29/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n29/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n29/r2.claim: Life loses its positive quality when pursued recklessly, without regard for spiritual values or the hereafter.

ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n30/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n30/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n30/r1.claim: The wording is literally, 'like the parable of ...'.

ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n31/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n31/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n31/r1.claim: This is the Qur'an's only use of kuffar in its original sense of tillers; Asad points to its etymology and the later sense of deniers in 74:10.

ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n32/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n32/r1.speaker: Tabari
ASAD-NOTES:57:20#n32/r1.claim: Tabari takes the conjunction wa here to mean aw, 'or'.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p168/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p168/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p168/r6.claim: The section laments people’s timid investment in transient worldly pleasure, which makes them forget their Lord’s mercy and the Paradise as vast as heaven and earth.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p183/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p183/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p183/r2.claim: The section warns wavering hypocrites of Jewish-like hardheartedness, then encourages trust in God’s power to revive faith as He revives dead earth; spending is never a loss, earns seventyfold reward, and can lead to ṣiddīq and shuhadā’ ranks.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p183/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p183/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p183/r3.claim: Ephemeral worldly attractions make people forget the eternal kingdom, which is as wide as the heavens and earth and can be bought with the pebbles they have collected.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p189/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p189/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p189/r5.claim: The verse warns wealth-enslaved hypocrites that worldly amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry for wealth, children, and status will not lead to a favorable end.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p189/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p189/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p189/r6.claim: Like rain that delights the ungrateful before its crop yellows and crumbles, worldly pleasures and competitive efforts all perish.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r1.claim: The foolish make worldly pleasure their goal, but the true goal is the Hereafter, where a person faces severe torment or God's forgiveness and acceptance; failure to win God's pleasure entails torment.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r2.speaker: exegetes
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r2.claim: The exegetes parse “the life of this world” as the subject and the remaining clause as its predicate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r3.claim: The author instead treats “sport, diversion, adornment” as an explanatory apposition and the rain simile as the predicate, citing a Qur'anic parallel.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r4.claim: Unlike the exegetes’ reading, the author's analysis does not condemn worldly life collectively; it condemns the worldly attachment that leads disbelievers and hypocrites to Hell, avoiding support for monasticism.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r5.claim: Worldly life itself is not condemnable: within God's limits it can secure the eternal Hereafter, while violating them and pursuing pleasure makes it eternal condemnation.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r6.speaker: exegetes
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r6.claim: Exegetes generally interpret kuffār here as farmers (zurrā‘).

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r7.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p190/r7.claim: The author rejects the rare farmer sense: root possibility alone cannot override customary Qur'anic usage when no other Qur'anic example supports it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p191/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p191/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p191/r1.claim: The author takes kuffār in its established sense of disbelievers, as 48:29 uses the term in its specific meanings; the transient world's lure targets those who disbelieve in the Hereafter.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p191/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p191/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-8-english:p191/r2.claim: A word in a simile can identify the people the comparison targets; recognizing this makes the parable's intended beauty evident.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r1.claim: Worldly life severed from humanity's created purpose loses meaning, but the Qur'an does not condemn life absolutely: it asks people to meet life's duties without forgetting that purpose.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r2.claim: Even an unbeliever can see that worldly actions with no intellectual link to the next life fade like rain-grown plants and finally become nothing.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r3.claim: The real comparison is with the plant, whose stages parallel human phases of play, amusement, acquiring property, and raising children.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r4.claim: Kuffar means “coverers”: farmers cover seed, while unbelievers conceal God and truth; the word may also hint at unbelievers' worldly attachment.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r5.speaker: İbn Âşûr
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r5.claim: The choice of kuffar for “farmers” may allude especially to disbelievers' attachment to worldly life.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r6.speaker: Taberî ve Şevkânî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r6.claim: The conjunction linking the Hereafter's outcomes marks alternatives: either severe punishment or God's forgiveness and approval.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:57:20/r7.claim: Accordingly, the phrase is rendered “either a severe punishment or forgiveness and approval from God.”

QIRAAT-ER:57:20:43#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:57:20:43#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:57:20:43#1/r1.claim: Riḍwān changes to ruḍwān with ḍamma; both are canonical and the source notes possible phonetic fullness.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r1.claim: Hayaja can describe growth in motion and then drying, but of vegetation it also means to dry; in this verse it means the crop dries and turns yellow.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r2.speaker: author
