SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r2.claim: The shift to you see it yellow makes the loss of adornment a matter of the observer's sight, since adornment is perceptual; the address applies to every onlooker.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p262/r3.claim: It becomes debris states an objective end with no use; seeing something as debris cannot establish its real value, which depends on knowledge rather than appearance.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p263/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p263/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p263/r1.claim: Seeing the crop yellow concerns its visible loss of beauty, while its becoming debris states the actual collapse of worldly life, not an observer's judgment.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p263/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p263/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p263/r2.claim: Fa marks immediate sequence, while thumma marks delay: the crop is seen yellow as soon as it dries, but becoming debris takes time; burial follows death promptly whereas resurrection is delayed.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p264/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p264/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p264/r1.claim: In Zumar, God is explicitly the agent who sends water, channels it, brings forth crops, and makes them debris; Hadid only compares worldly life to rain and leaves the agent unstated.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p265/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p265/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p265/r1.claim: Though both words refer to water from the sky, Quranic usage reserves matar for punishment and uses ghayth for beneficial rain; hadith usage can differ.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p266/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p266/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p266/r1.claim: Punishment precedes forgiveness because the gathering and passage by Hell occur before judgment and entry to Paradise; forgiveness then precedes divine approval in Paradise.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p266/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p266/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p266/r2.claim: The verse leaves the source of severe punishment unstated but attributes forgiveness to God, emphasizing His mercy; scripture avoids attributing evil to God.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p267/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p267/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p267/r1.claim: Ghufran appears only as a request for forgiveness from God, in Baqara 2:285; maghfira is not used as a prayer request and appears in statements about forgiveness.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p267/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p267/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p267/r2.claim: Unlike ghufran, maghfira can come from God or people; the Quran uses it in informative contexts, including forgiveness between people.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p268/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p268/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p268/r1.claim: Ridwan is used only of God and in both seeking and other contexts; mardat is used when seeking someone's pleasure and may concern God or another person.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p268/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p268/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p268/r2.claim: Ridwan is the broader term, while mardat is narrower and tied to seeking approval; this is a distinctive Quranic usage.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p269/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p269/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p269/r1.claim: After portraying worldly competition in play, boasting, adornment, and accumulation as ending in debris, God redirects people to compete for forgiveness and Paradise.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p271/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p271/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p271/r1.claim: The forgiveness in 57:20 is a description of worldly life's outcome, so it is from God; 57:21 addresses people with a command, so it says from your Lord.

STUDYQURAN:57:20/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r1.claim: Worldly wealth is relative, yet can be a cause for gratitude and should be managed properly.

STUDYQURAN:57:20/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r2.claim: Withering or failed crops serve elsewhere as metaphors for the relative and fleeting joys of worldly life.

STUDYQURAN:57:20/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r3.claim: Kuffar, translated here as farmers, can also mean disbelievers and could be rendered that way in this passage.

STUDYQURAN:57:20/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r4.claim: The statement that worldly life is delusive enjoyment is also found in other verses.

STUDYQURAN:57:20/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r5.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r5.claim: Ibn Ajibah says the world looks beautiful outside but hides ugliness within, gradually entangling its pursuers until they neglect preparation for the Hereafter.

STUDYQURAN:57:20/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:57:20/r6.claim: The discussion extends the surah's focus on the relationship between inward and outward appearances.
